decks.title: Sets — Part 1: Sets, subsets and intervals
goals: Decide when a collection is a set and write it in roster and set-builder form
Classify sets as empty, singleton, finite, infinite or equal
List subsets, count the power set and use the universal set
Write subsets of the real numbers in interval notation

slides.heading: Sets, Part 1: Collections with a clear rule
slides.body_md: A set is a collection whose membership is settled by a clear rule.

visual.caption: A set needs a rule that settles membership.

slides.narration: Welcome to Class Eleven mathematics, the course that begins with sets. A set is a collection of objects together with a rule that decides, for every object, whether it belongs. The distinct letters of a word form a set. The best songs of the decade do not, because best is an opinion. In this part you will write sets in several ways, classify them, and count their subsets.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Tell a **well-defined** collection from an opinion

visual.alt: Summary flow: a set is a well-defined collection; write it in roster, set-builder or interval form; classify it as empty, finite, infinite or equal to another; a set of n elements has 2 to the power n subsets.
visual.caption: From a collection to its subsets.

slides.narration: Here are your goals for part one. You will spot a genuine set, write it by listing or by a rule, and sort sets into types. Then you will study subsets and count them with a doubling rule. You will finish with intervals, the sets of real numbers that appear in nearly every later chapter of this course.

slides.heading: Elements and notation
slides.body_md: The objects of a set are its **elements**. Write $a \in A$ when $a$ belongs to $A$ and $a \notin A$ when it does not. Capital letters name sets. Five number sets have fixed names: $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{W}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$.

visual.alt: Flow diagram of the number sets, each inside the next: natural numbers inside whole numbers inside integers inside rational numbers inside real numbers.
visual.caption: Each number set is a subset of the next.

slides.narration: The objects in a set are called its elements. We use a rounded letter e symbol to say that an element belongs to a set, and the same symbol crossed out to say it does not. Capital letters name sets. Five number sets keep fixed names: natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers and real numbers. Each one sits inside the next, as the chain shows.

slides.heading: Roster form and set-builder form
slides.body_md: **Roster form** lists the elements: $\{12, 24, 36\}$. **Set-builder form** states a rule: $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \text{ is a multiple of } 12,\ x < 40\}$. List each element once; order does not matter.

rows: $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \text{ is a two-digit multiple of } 12\}$

visual.alt: Table converting four sets from set-builder to roster form: two-digit multiples of 12 give eight numbers from 12 to 96; integers whose square is below 20 give minus 4 to 4; divisors of 28 give six numbers; n times n plus 1 for n up to 4 gives 2, 6, 12, 20.
visual.caption: One set, two ways of writing it.

slides.narration: A set can be written in two ways. Roster form lists the elements between curly brackets. Set-builder form states the rule every element obeys, after a colon. The table converts four sets from rule to list. Look at the second row: the integers whose square is below twenty include negative numbers and zero, so always check which number system the rule lives in.

slides.heading: Quick check: is it a set?
slides.body_md: Pick the collection that a clear rule defines.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from rule to roster
slides.body_md: Write $A = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : -5 < 3x - 2 \le 10\}$ in roster form and find $n(A)$.
bullets: Integers in this range: $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ ($-1$ is excluded)

visual.alt: Table of the worked example: the inequality, its solution greater than minus 1 and at most 4, the integers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 that satisfy it, and the count 5.
visual.caption: Solve first, then list the integers allowed.

slides.narration: Treat the double inequality like an equation: add two to every part, then divide by three. The result says x is greater than minus one and at most four. Because minus one is not allowed, the integers start at zero and run up to four. Counting them gives five elements.

slides.heading: Types of sets
slides.body_md: **Empty set** $\varnothing$: no element. **Singleton**: one element. **Finite**: counting ends. **Infinite**: counting never ends. Note that $\{\varnothing\}$ is **not** empty; it has one element.

visual.alt: Table of the types of sets, one example each: an empty set with no element, a singleton with one element, a finite set of cubes below 100 with four elements, and an infinite set of integers below 5 that never ends.
visual.caption: Count the elements to decide the type.

slides.narration: Sets are classified by size. The empty set has no elements and is written with a slashed circle. A singleton has exactly one. A finite set can be counted to the end, and an infinite set cannot. A common trap: a set whose only element is the empty set is not itself empty, because it has one element inside the brackets.

slides.heading: Equal sets
slides.body_md: $A = B$ when they have exactly the same elements. Reordering or repeating elements changes nothing. Equal sets have equal counts, but equal counts do **not** make sets equal.

visual.alt: Table testing four sets against 2, 4, 6: the same elements in another order, with repeats, or described as even numbers below 7 are all equal to it; even numbers up to 8 include the extra element 8, so that set is different.
visual.caption: Order and repeats do not matter; the elements do.

slides.narration: Two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements. Writing them in another order, or repeating one, changes nothing. The table tests four descriptions against the set two, four, six. The last one has an extra element, eight, so it is a different set. Remember also that two sets can have the same number of elements without being equal.

slides.heading: Quick check: the empty set
slides.body_md: Is the set that contains only the empty set an empty set?

visual.alt: Table testing four sets against 2, 4, 6: the same elements in another order, with repeats, or described as even numbers below 7 are all equal to it; even numbers up to 8 include the extra element 8, so that set is different.
visual.caption: Order and repeats do not matter; the elements do.

slides.narration: Count the elements inside the outer brackets before you decide.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: classify and compare
slides.body_md: Let $A = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0\}$ and $B = \{x \in \mathbb{N} : x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0\}$. Write both in roster form and compare.
bullets: $B = \{4\}$: $-2$ is not natural, so $B$ is a singleton

visual.alt: Table comparing the two sets from the example: A is minus 2 and 4, with 2 elements; B is just 4, with 1 element, so B is a singleton that sits inside A.
visual.caption: Same equation, different universe, different set.

slides.narration: Both sets come from the same equation, which factorises with roots four and minus two. The difference is the universe. Among the integers, both roots count, so the first set has two elements. Among the natural numbers, minus two is not allowed, so the second set is a singleton holding only four. It is inside the first set but not equal to it.

slides.heading: Subsets
slides.body_md: $B \subseteq A$ if every element of $B$ is in $A$. If also $B \ne A$, then $B$ is a **proper subset**: $B \subset A$. The empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram inside a rectangle U of the numbers 1 to 10: a large circle A holds 2, 6, 10 and, inside it, a small circle B holds 4 and 8; the numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 lie outside both circles.
visual.caption: $B = \{4, 8\}$ lies inside $A = \{2, 4, 6, 8, 10\}$, so $B \subset A$.

slides.narration: A set B is a subset of A when every element of B is also in A. In the picture, the small circle inside the big one shows exactly this: four and eight belong to both. If B is not all of A, we call it a proper subset. Two facts to memorise: the empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself.

slides.heading: The power set
slides.body_md: The set of all subsets of $A$ is the **power set** $P(A)$. If $n(A) = n$, then $n(P(A)) = 2^n$, because each element is either in a subset or out of it.

visual.alt: Table listing all 8 subsets of p, q, r by size: one of size 0, the empty set; three of size 1; three of size 2; and one of size 3, the set itself. The counts 1, 3, 3, 1 add up to 8.
visual.caption: Total: $1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8 = 2^3$.

slides.narration: List every subset of the three element set p, q, r, sorted by size. There is one with no elements, three with one element, three with two elements, and one with all three. That makes eight. The reason is simple: each element is either in or out, two choices for each, so three elements give two times two times two.

slides.heading: Subsets double with each new element
slides.body_md: Subsets: $2^n$. Proper subsets: $2^n - 1$. Non-empty proper subsets: $2^n - 2$.

visual.alt: Table of the number of subsets of a set with 0 to 6 elements: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, doubling each time; the proper subsets are one fewer in each column.
visual.caption: Each new element doubles the count: $2^n$.

slides.narration: Here is the doubling in numbers. A set with no elements has one subset, itself. Add one element and the count doubles to two, then four, eight, sixteen, thirty two, sixty four. Take away the set itself to count proper subsets, and take away the empty set as well to count the non-empty proper subsets. These three counts appear again and again.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: counting with conditions
slides.body_md: How many subsets of $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ contain $2$ but not $5$?
bullets: $2$ must be in, $5$ must be out
The other four elements $1, 3, 4, 6$ are free

visual.alt: Table for the worked example: element 2 is forced in, one way; element 5 is forced out, one way; elements 1, 3, 4, 6 are free, 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 ways; the total is 16 subsets.
visual.caption: Forced elements add no choice.

slides.narration: When some elements are forced in or forced out, only the remaining elements give a choice. Here two must be in and five must be out, so each has just one way. The four other elements are each in or out, giving two to the fourth power, which is sixteen subsets. Listing all sixty four subsets by computer confirms the count.

slides.heading: Quick check: counting subsets
slides.body_md: Fill in the number of subsets of a set with seven elements.

visual.alt: Table of the number of subsets of a set with 0 to 6 elements: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, doubling each time; the proper subsets are one fewer in each column.
visual.caption: Each new element doubles the count: $2^n$.

slides.narration: Use the doubling rule with seven elements, and remember the empty set and the set itself both count.

slides.heading: Universal set
slides.body_md: Within one problem, every set is a subset of a fixed **universal set** $U$, drawn as a rectangle. Circles inside the rectangle represent subsets of $U$.

visual.alt: A rectangle U holding the numbers 1 to 9 with one circle A around 3, 6 and 9; the remaining numbers 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8 lie inside the rectangle but outside the circle.
visual.caption: The universal set $U = \{1, 2, \dots, 9\}$ is the rectangle; $A$ is the circle of multiples of $3$.

slides.narration: In any problem, all the sets live inside one larger set called the universal set. We draw it as a rectangle and draw each set as a circle inside it. Here the universal set is the numbers one to nine and the circle holds the multiples of three. The numbers left outside the circle, but inside the rectangle, are the ones that are not multiples of three.

slides.heading: Intervals of real numbers
slides.body_md: Intervals are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. A **square** bracket includes the end point; a **round** bracket excludes it. The symbol $\infty$ is not a number, so it always gets a round bracket.

visual.alt: Table pairing four set-builder descriptions with interval notation: the open interval from minus 1 to 4, the closed interval, the half-open interval that includes 4, and the unbounded interval of numbers up to 4.
visual.caption: Round bracket: excluded. Square bracket: included.

slides.narration: Sets of real numbers between two end points are called intervals. A square bracket means the end point is included, and a round bracket means it is excluded. The symbol for infinity always gets a round bracket, because infinity is not a number you can reach. The table matches four descriptions with their interval notation.

slides.heading: Intervals on the number line
slides.body_md: Filled circle: included. Open circle: excluded. Arrow: continues for ever.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: A set is a well-defined collection; roster form and set-builder form
Empty, singleton, finite, infinite; equal sets have the same elements
Subset, proper subset, universal set; $\varnothing \subseteq A$ always
Intervals: square bracket included, round bracket excluded

visual.alt: Summary flow: a set is a well-defined collection; write it in roster, set-builder or interval form; classify it as empty, finite, infinite or equal to another; a set of n elements has 2 to the power n subsets.
visual.caption: From a collection to its subsets.

slides.narration: To sum up. A set is a well defined collection, written by listing or by a rule. Sets can be empty, finite, infinite or equal. A subset has all its elements in the larger set, and a set with n elements has two to the power n subsets. Finally, intervals are sets of real numbers, with square brackets for included ends and round brackets for excluded ends.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Roster form (1 to 2 marks):** solve the condition in the stated universe, then list every element once
**Subset counts (1 to 3 marks):** state $2^n$ and the reason, fixing forced elements first
**Intervals (1 to 2 marks):** each end-point bracket is marked; a wrong bracket loses the mark
**Mistakes:** dropping negative integers or $0$ when the universe is $\mathbb{Z}$; a square bracket beside $\infty$
slides.narration: In the school examination, marks go to the roster form with every element listed once, to the power of two count with its reason, and to the correct bracket at each end of an interval. Common slips are calling a set that holds the empty set empty, forgetting negative integers and zero, and putting a square bracket next to infinity. Always solve the condition inside the universe the question names.

decks.title: Sets — Part 2: Operations, laws and counting
goals: Find union, intersection, difference and complement from sets and Venn diagrams
Use the laws of set algebra, including De Morgan's laws
Operate on intervals of real numbers
Solve word problems on the number of elements in unions of two and three sets

slides.heading: Sets, Part 2: Combining sets
slides.body_md: Union, intersection, difference and complement build new sets from old ones.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of U equal to 1 to 12 with two overlapping circles: A holds the factors of 24, which are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, and B holds the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. Only A has 1, 4, 6, 8, 12; the overlap has 2 and 3; only B has 5, 7, 11; 9 and 10 lie outside.
visual.caption: $A$ = factors of $24$ and $B$ = primes, inside $U = \{1, \dots, 12\}$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Two sets overlap in a Venn diagram: the factors of twenty four and the primes up to twelve. Two and three belong to both. You will combine sets in four ways, learn the laws that let you rewrite expressions, and use Venn diagrams to turn word problems into simple counting.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Read the regions of a **Venn diagram**
Count with $n(A \cup B)$ and $n(A \cup B \cup C)$

nodes.label: Three sets: singles, minus pairs, plus triple

visual.alt: Summary flow: the four operations; the laws including De Morgan; the two-set counting formula; the three-set counting formula.
visual.caption: From operations to counting.

slides.narration: Here are your goals for part two. You will compute the four operations from lists and diagrams, apply the laws of set algebra, combine intervals on the number line, and solve practical counting problems with the union formula for two sets and for three sets.

slides.heading: Union and intersection
slides.body_md: $A \cup B$: elements in $A$ **or** $B$ (or both). $A \cap B$: elements in **both**. If $A \cap B = \varnothing$ the sets are **disjoint**.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of U equal to 1 to 12 with two overlapping circles: A holds the factors of 24, which are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, and B holds the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. Only A has 1, 4, 6, 8, 12; the overlap has 2 and 3; only B has 5, 7, 11; 9 and 10 lie outside.
visual.caption: $A$ = factors of $24$ and $B$ = primes, inside $U = \{1, \dots, 12\}$.

math: A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}, \quad A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}
slides.narration: The union of two sets collects everything that is in the first, or the second, or both. The intersection keeps only what is in both. In the diagram the union is all three coloured regions, and the intersection is the overlap, which holds two and three. Elements that appear in both sets are still listed only once in the union.

slides.heading: Disjoint sets
slides.body_md: Sets with no common element are **disjoint**: their circles do not overlap and $M \cap P = \varnothing$.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of U equal to 1 to 10 with two separate circles that do not touch: M holds the squares 1, 4, 9 and P holds the primes 2, 3, 5, 7. The numbers 6, 8 and 10 lie outside both. No number is in both circles.
visual.caption: Disjoint sets: $M \cap P = \varnothing$.

slides.narration: Sometimes two sets share nothing. The squares one, four, nine and the primes two, three, five, seven are an example. Their circles do not touch, and their intersection is the empty set. Disjoint sets matter in counting, because the size of their union is simply the sum of the two sizes.

slides.heading: Difference
slides.body_md: $A - B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \notin B\}$. In general $A - B \ne B - A$.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of U equal to 1 to 12 with two overlapping circles: A holds the factors of 24, which are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, and B holds the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. Only A has 1, 4, 6, 8, 12; the overlap has 2 and 3; only B has 5, 7, 11; 9 and 10 lie outside.
visual.caption: $A$ = factors of $24$ and $B$ = primes, inside $U = \{1, \dots, 12\}$.

slides.narration: The difference of A and B keeps the elements of A that are not in B. Here A minus B is one, four, six, eight and twelve, the factors of twenty four that are not prime. B minus A is five, seven and eleven. The order matters: the two differences are different sets, one on each side of the overlap.

slides.heading: Complement
slides.body_md: $A' = U - A$: everything in $U$ that is **not** in $A$. Then $A \cup A' = U$ and $A \cap A' = \varnothing$.

visual.alt: A rectangle U holding 1 to 12 with a circle A around the factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12. The complement of A is everything in the rectangle outside the circle: 5, 7, 9, 10, 11.
visual.caption: The complement $A' = U - A$ is everything outside the circle.

slides.narration: The complement of a set is everything in the universal set that lies outside it, so it depends on the universal set you chose. For the factors of twenty four inside the numbers one to twelve, the complement is five, seven, nine, ten and eleven. A set and its complement together make the whole universal set, and they have nothing in common.

slides.heading: Quick check: a difference as an intersection
slides.body_md: Which set equals $A \cap B'$?

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of U equal to 1 to 12 with two overlapping circles: A holds the factors of 24, which are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, and B holds the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. Only A has 1, 4, 6, 8, 12; the overlap has 2 and 3; only B has 5, 7, 11; 9 and 10 lie outside.
visual.caption: $A$ = factors of $24$ and $B$ = primes, inside $U = \{1, \dots, 12\}$.

slides.narration: Translate the symbols into words: in A, and not in B.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: seven operations
slides.body_md: For $U = \{1, \dots, 12\}$, $A$ = factors of $24$ and $B$ = primes, find $A \cup B$, $A \cap B$, $A - B$, $B - A$, $A'$, $(A \cup B)'$ and $(A \cap B)'$.
bullets: Complements: from the numbers outside the regions

visual.alt: Table of seven operations on A and B inside U of 1 to 12: the union has 10 elements, the intersection 2, A minus B 5, B minus A 3, the complement of A 5, the complement of the union 2, and the complement of the intersection 10.
visual.caption: Each result is read from the regions.

slides.narration: Work from the diagram. The union lists ten numbers. The intersection is two and three. The two differences are one, four, six, eight, twelve on one side and five, seven, eleven on the other. The complement of the union is nine and ten, only two numbers, while the complement of the intersection contains everything except two and three. Every result is read straight from a region.

slides.heading: Laws of set algebra
slides.body_md: Union and intersection are **commutative** and **associative**, and each **distributes** over the other. Identity, complement and difference rules also hold. Each rule in the table was tested on every triple of subsets of a four-element set.

headers: Tested on every triple of subsets of $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$
rows: $A \cup B = B \cup A$ and $A \cap B = B \cap A$

visual.alt: Table of nine rules of set algebra: commutative, associative, two distributive laws, two De Morgan laws, identity, complement and difference, each with a tick showing it was tested on every triple of subsets of 1, 2, 3, 4.
visual.caption: Every rule passed the brute-force test.

slides.narration: Set operations obey laws much like those for numbers. Union and intersection can be swapped, regrouped, and each distributes over the other. There are identity laws with the empty set and the universal set, a complement law, and the useful rewrite of a difference as an intersection with a complement. The table lists nine rules, and each passed a test on every possible triple of subsets of a four element set.

slides.heading: De Morgan's laws
slides.body_md: $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ and $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$. A complement swaps union and intersection.

visual.alt: Table of the four regions of a two-circle Venn diagram. Only the region outside both circles lies in the complement of the union, and only that region lies in both complements, so the two sets are the same.
visual.caption: The last two columns match in every row: De Morgan.

slides.narration: De Morgan laws tell you how a complement passes through a union or an intersection. Not in A or B means not in A and not in B. The table checks the four regions of a two circle diagram. Only the region outside both circles belongs to the complement of the union, and only that region belongs to both complements, so the two sets are the same.

slides.heading: Quick check: complements and subsets
slides.body_md: If $A \subseteq B$, how do $A'$ and $B'$ compare?

visual.alt: Table of the four regions of a two-circle Venn diagram. Only the region outside both circles lies in the complement of the union, and only that region lies in both complements, so the two sets are the same.
visual.caption: The last two columns match in every row: De Morgan.

slides.narration: Think about an element outside B. Can it be inside A?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: verify a law
slides.body_md: With $U = \{1, \dots, 12\}$, $A$ = factors of $24$, $B$ = primes, verify $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$.

visual.alt: Table verifying one De Morgan law: the union of A and B has ten elements, its complement is 9 and 10, and the intersection of the two complements is also 9 and 10.
visual.caption: Both sides give the same set.

slides.narration: To verify a law with numbers, compute each side separately and compare. The union of A and B has ten elements, so its complement in one to twelve is just nine and ten. The complements of A and B are bigger sets, but their common part is again nine and ten. The two sides agree, as the law predicts.

slides.heading: Intervals: union, intersection, difference
slides.body_md: $A = (-5, 1]$, $B = [-2, 4)$. Test every end point in **both** sets.

slides.narration: Operations work on intervals as well. Take A, from minus five excluded to one included, and B, from minus two included to four excluded. The intersection runs from minus two to one with both ends included, because minus two is in A and one is in B. The union runs from minus five to four with both ends open. The difference A minus B stops just short of minus two.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: interval end points
slides.body_md: For the intervals above, find $A \cap B$, $A \cup B$, $A - B$ and $B - A$.
bullets: $A - B = (-5, -2)$: $-2 \in B$, so it is removed
$B - A = (1, 4)$: $1 \in A$, so it is removed

visual.alt: Table of the four interval results with their end points: the intersection from minus 2 to 1 has both ends included; the union from minus 5 to 4, the difference A minus B from minus 5 to minus 2, and B minus A from 1 to 4 all have both ends excluded.
visual.caption: Decide every end point by testing it in both sets.

slides.narration: The method never changes. Find the end points and test each one in both sets. Minus two is in A and in B, so it stays in the intersection. For the union, minus five is not in A and four is not in B, so both ends are open. For the difference, minus two belongs to B, so it is removed from A minus B, which therefore stays open there.

slides.heading: Counting two sets
slides.body_md: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. Also $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$ and $n(A') = n(U) - n(A)$.

visual.caption: Region counts: $55 + 30 + 42 + 23 = 150$.

math: n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)
slides.narration: To count a union, add the two sizes and subtract the overlap, because the overlap was counted twice. In the example, among one hundred fifty people, eighty five like tea and seventy two like coffee, and thirty like both. The diagram shows the four region counts, which add up to the total.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a word problem
slides.body_md: Of $150$ people, $85$ like tea, $72$ like coffee and $30$ like both. How many like at least one, only tea, neither?

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of 150 people with two overlapping circles: T for tea with 85 people and C for coffee with 72. Only tea has 55, the overlap has 30, only coffee has 42, and 23 lie outside both circles.
visual.caption: Region counts: $55 + 30 + 42 + 23 = 150$.

slides.narration: Start with the union formula: eighty five plus seventy two minus thirty gives one hundred twenty seven people who like at least one drink. Only tea is eighty five minus the overlap, which is fifty five. Those who like neither form the complement of the union: one hundred fifty minus one hundred twenty seven, twenty three. The diagram confirms all four regions.

slides.heading: Quick check: a union count
slides.body_md: Count the books in both languages from the totals.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of 150 people with two overlapping circles: T for tea with 85 people and C for coffee with 72. Only tea has 55, the overlap has 30, only coffee has 42, and 23 lie outside both circles.
visual.caption: Region counts: $55 + 30 + 42 + 23 = 150$.

slides.narration: Every book is in at least one language, so the union equals the total. Then solve the union formula for the overlap.

slides.heading: Counting three sets
slides.body_md: $n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cap B) - n(B \cap C) - n(A \cap C) + n(A \cap B \cap C)$. Fill the Venn regions from the centre outwards.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of 60 learners with three overlapping circles A, B and C. The centre holds 4; the pairwise-only regions hold 6, 5 and 7; the single-set regions hold 12, 10 and 9; 7 lie outside all three circles.
visual.caption: The regions add to $60$; $n(A \cup B \cup C) = 53$.

slides.narration: For three sets, add the three sizes, subtract the three pairwise overlaps, then add back the triple overlap, which was removed once too often. In the diagram, fill the centre first, then the pair only regions, then the single regions. The three circles together hold fifty three of sixty learners, and seven lie outside all of them.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: three sets
slides.body_md: Using $n(A) = 29$, $n(B) = 25$, $n(C) = 25$, $n(A \cap B) = 10$, $n(B \cap C) = 9$, $n(A \cap C) = 11$, $n(A \cap B \cap C) = 4$ and $n(U) = 60$, find the learners in none of the sets and in exactly one set.

visual.alt: Table of region counts for the three-set example: only A 12, only B 10, only C 9, so exactly one set holds 31 learners, and 7 learners lie in none of the sets.
visual.caption: Add the single-set regions for exactly one.

slides.narration: First the union: add the three sizes, subtract the three pair overlaps, add the triple overlap, and you get fifty three. So seven learners are in none of the sets. To find those in exactly one set, subtract from each size the parts shared with the other sets, adding the triple back once. That gives twelve, ten and nine, which total thirty one.

Laws: commutative, associative, distributive, identity, complement, De Morgan
Intervals: test every end point in both sets

slides.narration: To sum up. The four operations come straight from Venn regions. The laws, especially De Morgan, let you rewrite expressions. On intervals, test each end point in both sets. For counting, add the sizes and subtract the overlap, and for three sets add back the triple overlap at the end.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Verify a law (2 to 3 marks):** compute both sides separately, then state that they are equal
**Prove an identity (2 to 5 marks):** two inclusions, each with a general element $x$
**Intervals:** one mark for each correct end-point decision
**Word problems (3 to 5 marks):** formula or Venn diagram, then each region or total
**Mistakes:** treating $A - B$ as $B - A$; counting the overlap twice; taking a complement in the wrong universal set
slides.narration: In the school examination, verification questions give a mark for each side computed and one for the conclusion. Proofs of identities need both inclusions, written with a general element. Interval answers are marked end point by end point. Word problems earn marks for the method and for each region or total. Common slips are swapping the two differences, miscounting the overlap, and taking a complement in the wrong universal set.

sections.heading: 1. Sets and their representations
sections.body_md:
A **set** is a well-defined collection of objects; the objects are its **elements**. $a \in A$ means $a$ belongs to $A$.

- **Roster form:** list the elements once each, e.g. $\{12, 24, 36, 48\}$.
- **Set-builder form:** give a rule, e.g. $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \text{ is a two-digit multiple of } 12\}$.

Standard sets: $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{W}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$, each inside the next. Solve a set-builder condition inside the stated universe (negative integers and $0$ count in $\mathbb{Z}$).

key_terms.definition_md: A well-defined collection: a clear rule settles membership.
An object in a set; $a \in A$.
The set written by listing its elements once each.
The set written by a rule its elements satisfy.

sections.heading: 2. Empty, finite, infinite and equal sets
sections.body_md:
- **Empty set** $\varnothing$: no element. $\{\varnothing\}$ is **not** empty; it has one element.
- **Singleton:** exactly one element.
- **Finite:** counting ends; $n(A)$ is the number of elements.
- **Infinite:** counting never ends.
- **Equal sets:** exactly the same elements. Order and repeats do not matter; equal counts do not make equal sets.

The same equation can give different sets in different universes: $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$ gives $\{-2, 4\}$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ but $\{4\}$ in $\mathbb{N}$.

sections.heading: 3. Subsets, power set and universal set
sections.body_md:
$B \subseteq A$ if every element of $B$ is in $A$; $B \subset A$ if also $B \ne A$ (**proper** subset). $\varnothing \subseteq A$ and $A \subseteq A$ always.

The **power set** $P(A)$ is the set of all subsets. If $n(A) = n$: subsets $2^n$; proper subsets $2^n - 1$; non-empty proper subsets $2^n - 2$. Forcing $k$ elements in or out leaves $2^{n-k}$ subsets.

The **universal set** $U$ contains every set of the discussion; it is the rectangle of a Venn diagram.

key_terms.definition_md: $B \subseteq A$: every element of $B$ is in $A$.
$P(A)$: the set of all subsets of $A$.
The set $U$ of which all sets under discussion are subsets.

sections.heading: 4. Intervals of real numbers
sections.body_md:
Intervals are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. $(a, b)$ excludes both ends; $[a, b]$ includes both; $[a, b)$ and $(a, b]$ include one. $(a, \infty)$ and $(-\infty, b]$ are unbounded. $\infty$ is never included.

On the number line: filled circle = included, open circle = excluded.

Integers in an interval depend on the ends: $(-1, 4)$ has $4$, $[-1, 4]$ has $6$, $(-1, 4]$ has $5$.

sections.heading: 5. Venn diagrams and operations
sections.body_md:
- **Union** $A \cup B$: in $A$ or $B$ (or both).
- **Intersection** $A \cap B$: in both. **Disjoint** if $A \cap B = \varnothing$.
- **Difference** $A - B$: in $A$, not in $B$; in general $A - B \ne B - A$.
- **Complement** $A' = U - A$.

In a Venn diagram, label the regions: only $A$, both, only $B$, outside. For intervals, test every end point in both sets: $(-5, 1] \cap [-2, 4) = [-2, 1]$ and $(-5, 1] \cup [-2, 4) = (-5, 4)$.

key_terms.definition_md: All elements of either set, each listed once.
The elements common to both sets.
$A' = U - A$, the elements of $U$ not in $A$.

sections.heading: 6. Laws of set algebra and De Morgan
sections.body_md:
- **Commutative:** $A \cup B = B \cup A$, $A \cap B = B \cap A$.
- **Associative:** $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$, and the same for $\cap$.
- **Distributive:** $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$, $A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$.
- **De Morgan:** $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$, $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$.
- **Identity and complement:** $A \cup \varnothing = A$, $A \cap U = A$, $A \cup A' = U$, $A \cap A' = \varnothing$; also $(A')' = A$.

To **verify** a law, compute both sides for the given sets. To **prove** an identity, show each side is a subset of the other using a general element $x$.

$n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$, $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$, $n(A') = n(U) - n(A)$. For disjoint sets, $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B)$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded** (school examination, Paper I: Sets and Functions together carry 18 of the 80 marks)
- *Objective items (1 mark each):* one mark for the correct option, so read every option.
- *Roster and set-builder (2 marks):* solve the condition in the stated universe, then list each element once.
- *Subset counts (2 to 3 marks):* $2^n$ with the reason; forced elements first.
- *Verify a law (3 marks):* each side computed separately, then the conclusion.
- *Prove an identity (2 to 3 marks):* each inclusion with a general $x$, then the conclusion.
- *Intervals (2 to 3 marks):* one mark for each correct end-point decision.
- *Long answer (5 marks, set in parts):* word problems and multi-part verifications; show the formula or the Venn regions.

**Common mistakes**
1. Calling $\{\varnothing\}$ the empty set.
2. Leaving out negative integers or $0$ when the universe is $\mathbb{Z}$.
3. Treating $A - B$ as $B - A$.
4. Writing a square bracket next to $\infty$.
5. Counting the overlap twice in $n(A \cup B)$.
6. Taking a complement in the wrong universal set.
7. Proving a set identity with one example instead of a general element.
8. Forgetting that the empty set and the set itself are both subsets.

questions.stem_md: Exactly one of the four collections below is decided by a clear rule rather than by opinion, so it forms a set. Which one is it?

options.text_md: The months of a year that have exactly $30$ days
The kindest teachers of a school
The most beautiful monuments of Rajasthan
The most interesting chapters in a mathematics book

questions.solution_md: A set needs a rule that settles membership for every object. Exactly $30$ days gives April, June, September and November. "Most interesting", "kindest" and "most beautiful" are opinions.

questions.stem_md: Written in roster form, the set $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \text{ is a factor of } 30 \text{ and } x \text{ is odd}\}$ is
questions.solution_md: The factors of $30$ are $1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30$. Keeping the odd ones leaves $1, 3, 5, 15$. Listing all eight ignores "odd"; the other two sets drop a factor.

questions.stem_md: How many integers $x$ satisfy $-30 < x^3 < 30$?
questions.solution_md: $3^3 = 27 < 30$ but $4^3 = 64 > 30$, so $x$ runs from $-3$ to $3$: seven integers. Stopping at $\pm 2$ gives $5$; leaving out $0$ gives $6$.

questions.stem_md: Exactly one of the following sets is empty. Which one?
questions.solution_md: $x^2 - 6x + 10 = (x - 3)^2 + 1 \ge 1$, so it is never $0$ and the first set is empty. The others hold $\pm 5$, $\dfrac14$ and $3$.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of sets consists of two equal sets?
questions.solution_md: The natural numbers below $5$ are exactly $1, 2, 3, 4$. In the others, $x^2 = 4$ gives $-2$ and $2$; $9$ is not prime; and $x^2 = x$ gives $0$ and $1$.

questions.stem_md: A set has exactly $256$ subsets. How many elements does it have?
questions.solution_md: A set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets, and $2^8 = 256$, so $n = 8$.

questions.stem_md: Set $A$ has $2$ more elements than set $B$, and $n(P(A)) - n(P(B)) = 96$, where $P$ stands for the power set. Then $n(A)$ equals
questions.solution_md: Let $n(B) = n$. Then $2^{n + 2} - 2^n = 3 \cdot 2^n = 96$, so $2^n = 32$ and $n = 5$. Hence $n(A) = 7$. The value $5$ is $n(B)$.

questions.stem_md: Let $A = \{1, 2, \{3, 4\}\}$, a set that has another set as one of its elements. Which statement is true?
questions.solution_md: The set $\{3, 4\}$ is itself one of the three elements of $A$, so it belongs to $A$. It is not a subset, because $3 \notin A$; and $n(A) = 3$, not $4$.

questions.stem_md: In interval notation, the set $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x < -2\}$ is written as
questions.solution_md: The numbers are all below $-2$ and $-2$ itself is excluded, so the bracket at $-2$ is round. A square bracket never goes next to $\infty$.

questions.stem_md: How many integers lie in the interval $[-6, -1)$?
questions.solution_md: $-6$ is included and $-1$ is excluded, so the integers are $-6, -5, -4, -3, -2$: five of them. Including $-1$ as well would give $6$.

questions.stem_md: For $U = \{1, 2, \dots, 30\}$, let $A$ hold the multiples of $3$ and $B$ the multiples of $5$. Then $n(A \cup B)$ is
questions.solution_md: $n(A) = 10$, $n(B) = 6$, and the common multiples are $15$ and $30$, so $n(A \cap B) = 2$. Then $n(A \cup B) = 10 + 6 - 2 = 14$. The value $16$ forgets the overlap.

For subsets of a universal set $U$, the set $A \cap B'$ is the same as
questions.solution_md: An element of $A \cap B'$ is in $A$ and not in $B$, which is the definition of $A - B$. The set $B - A$ is $B \cap A'$, the mirror image.

questions.stem_md: Three sets satisfy $A \cap B = A \cap C$ and $A \cup B = A \cup C$. Which conclusion must hold?
questions.solution_md: An element of $B$ outside $A$ lies in $A \cup B = A \cup C$, so it lies in $C$; an element of $B$ inside $A$ lies in $A \cap B = A \cap C$, so again in $C$. Hence $B \subseteq C$, and by symmetry $B = C$. The other three fail for $A = \varnothing$, $B = C = \{1\}$.

questions.stem_md: Each of the $45$ books on a shelf is in English, in Hindi, or in both languages. Of them, $30$ are in English and $25$ are in Hindi. How many books are in both languages?
questions.solution_md: Every book is counted at least once, so $n(E \cup H) = 45$. Then $45 = 30 + 25 - n(E \cap H)$ gives $n(E \cap H) = 55 - 45 = 10$. The value $55$ is the plain sum.

questions.stem_md: According to De Morgan's law for an intersection, $(A \cap B)'$ is equal to
questions.solution_md: An element outside $A \cap B$ fails to be in $A$ or fails to be in $B$, so it lies in $A'$ or in $B'$: $A' \cup B'$. The set $A' \cap B'$ equals $(A \cup B)'$, the other law.

questions.stem_md: For finite sets $A$ and $B$, $n(A) = 47$, $n(B) = 32$ and $n(A \cap B) = 19$. How many elements belong to exactly one of the two sets?
questions.solution_md: Only $A$: $47 - 19 = 28$. Only $B$: $32 - 19 = 13$. Exactly one: $28 + 13 = 41$. The value $60$ counts the overlap once as well, and $79$ is the plain sum.

questions.stem_md: How many subsets of $\{1, 2, \dots, 7\}$ have only even numbers as elements? The empty set is counted.
questions.solution_md: The even numbers available are $2, 4, 6$. Each is in or out, so there are $2^3 = 8$ such subsets, including $\varnothing$.

questions.stem_md: The intervals $A = [-4, 1)$ and $B = (-2, 6]$ lie on the real line. Their intersection $A \cap B$ is
questions.solution_md: The overlap starts just above $-2$ because $-2 \notin B$, and stops just below $1$ because $1 \notin A$. Both end points are excluded: $(-2, 1)$.

questions.solution_md: $-1$ belongs to $[-1, 3)$, so it is not in the complement; $3$ does not belong, so it is in the complement. That gives a round bracket at $-1$ and a square bracket at $3$.

(a) For finite sets $A$ and $B$, split $A \cup B$ into the three disjoint parts $A - B$, $A \cap B$ and $B - A$, and use them to prove that $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$.

(b) Each of $40$ pupils in an imagined class plays chess, carrom or both; $28$ play chess and $19$ play carrom. How many play both? How many play only carrom?

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The sets $A - B$, $A \cap B$ and $B - A$ have no element in common and together make $A \cup B$, so $n(A \cup B) = n(A - B) + n(A \cap B) + n(B - A)$.

Also $A$ is split into $A - B$ and $A \cap B$, so $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$; similarly $n(B - A) = n(B) - n(A \cap B)$.

Substituting, $n(A \cup B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B) + n(A \cap B) + n(B) - n(A \cap B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$.

**(b)** Everyone plays at least one game, so $n(\text{chess} \cup \text{carrom}) = 40$. Then $40 = 28 + 19 - n(\text{both})$ gives $n(\text{both}) = 47 - 40 = 7$.

Only carrom: $19 - 7 = 12$.

questions.solution_md: Split into disjoint parts, then substitute; part (b) is the formula solved for the overlap.

marking_scheme.step: n(A - B) and n(B - A) in terms of the overlap

questions.stem_md:
Let $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : -3 \le x \le 3\}$, $T = \{x^2 : x \in S\}$ and $W = \{x \in S : x^2 \le 4\}$.

(a) Write $T$ and $W$ in roster form.

(b) State, with a reason, whether $W \subset S$ and whether $T \subseteq S$.

(c) Find $T \cap W$ and the number of subsets of $T \cap W$.

(d) Find $T - W$ and $S - W$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Squares of $-3, \dots, 3$ are $9, 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, 9$; listing each once gives $T = \{0, 1, 4, 9\}$. The integers with $x^2 \le 4$ are $W = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$.

**(b)** Every element of $W$ is in $S$ and $W \ne S$ (it lacks $3$), so $W \subset S$. But $9 \in T$ and $9 \notin S$, so $T \subseteq S$ is false.

**(c)** $T \cap W = \{0, 1\}$. It has $2$ elements, so it has $2^2 = 4$ subsets.

**(d)** $T - W = \{4, 9\}$ and $S - W = \{-3, 3\}$.

(b) W proper subset of S; T not a subset of S
